HOME INTRUDER SHOOTINGS

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A Home Intruder Shooting is not always straight-forward self-defenses scenario – pulling the trigger could land you behind bars.

Unique Selling Point:
TOPICAL & RELEVANT TO VIEWERS

Summary:
With armed home robberies up by 7.3% in last year’s National Crime Statistics, South Africans are stepping up to defend their families and their homes.

But self-defense is not a get out of jail free claim – you could actually end up behind bars if you act outside of the law.

We ask where is the line and when do you cross it according to the law.


Further information:
With a spate of home intruder shootings, we explore the legal debate around what is considered self-defense and what is murder in the eyes of the law.

We explore the current state of house robberies in South Africa, looking at this rising crime trend and driving forces behind it.

A number of the intruders that have been killed have been identified as criminals that have been released from prison just weeks before committing the crimes that lead to their death. We look at what appears to be a vicious crime circle, where criminals get caught, justice is thought to be served, yet the criminals continue to perpetrate more crimes.

EXPERT INTERVIEWS
- Gareth Newham – ISS – will paint the picture of current crime trend, driving forces and why South Africans are so desperately vulnerable in the context of violent crime.
- Lobo das Neves – Law Enforcement Expert – will explain how people react, how they should react – and expand on the flight or fright theories.
- Advocate John Welch – legal expert – will explain the legal framework, what action can be taken and what the consequences are for homeowners who shoot outside of the law.

CASE STUDIES
There are at least 5 cases since January this year of intruders being shot by residents of the homes that were being burgled.

In some cases the home owners have been charged, in some cases where there were clear cases of self-defense no charges were laid.

Some of the more recent case studies are either too traumatized to speak or are concerned about the pending criminal investigations.

CASE STUDY PORT SHEPSTONE
February 8, 2018
Two men armed with knives and a screw-driver broke into a home in Park Road, Umtentweni during the early hours.
Neil and Lynn-Dee van Eeden and their 17-year-old son, Josh were sleeping when the men quietly cut the burglar bars with bolt-cutters and climbed through the lounge window into the house and proceeded to make their way down the passage and into Neil’s bedroom.
Neil woke-up with the two men, wearing hats, in his bedroom, telling him to ‘keep cool’. One of the men had one of Neil’s socks wrapped around his face.
When the family’s boerboel come through to the bedroom, the intruders attempted to stab the dog.
A calm Neil asked the men if he could put the dog in his bedroom. They agreed, and made their way to Joshua’s room where they helped themselves to his laptop and cellphone.
They demanded money, and asked Neil for a bag.
When the men realised they had taken only one of a pair of takkies, they insisted that Neil retrieve the other from the bedroom.
Deciding enough was enough, Neil went back into his bedroom, closed the door to keep the dogs inside, and took his gun from the safe.
When the intruder saw the gun, he went for me and that’s when I shot him. This is what worried me – if they couldn’t find money what would they have done, tied us up and slit our throats? – Neil.
Neil said the injured man stumbled back and fell into Josh’s room, where he lay for a while.
The wounded man staggered into Josh’s room, were he lay for a while.
The other man, who was busy filling the bag with laptops, clothes and other household goods, abandoned the bag, opened the sliding door in the lounge and fled.
By this time, Lynn-Dee had emerged from her bedroom to see the wounded man stumbling down the passage, shouting ‘please don’t shoot me, please don’t shoot me…’
“Out of sheer fright, Josh and I grabbed coffee cups and threw them at him,” said Lynn-Dee.
Lynn-Dee phoned her level-headed friend Sally Heaver for help, just before 3am.
The missing takkie which provided the chance for Neil to retrieve his firearm.
Sally in turn quickly contacted the police and posted a message on a local WhatsApp group saying the family needed help.
Police spokesman, Vincent Pandarum said the wounded man had managed to run a few hundred metres before collapsing and dying.
Reflecting on the ordeal, Lynn-Dee said the men were starting to get aggressive as things weren’t going as planned – suddenly there were dogs, no money, not everyone in the same room and it was taking longer than anticipated.
One of the coffee cups thrown at the intruder.
Josh hadn’t seen his mother during this ordeal and was worried that she had been targeted.
“It could have been so much worse,” added Josh.
Capt Pandarum said a case of house robbery would be investigated, and an inquest docket opened in relation to the death of the suspect.
No arrests have been made at this stage.

Mr. Gareth Newhm INSTITUTE FOR SECURITY STUDIES
Mr. Lobo das Neves
Mr. ADVOCATE JOHN WELCH ADVOCATE

Press Release:


Home Intruder Shootings
Approximately 60 house burglaries take place in South Africa every day and research shows that home invasions are one of the most feared crimes in the country. Increasingly, home owners are stepping up and using force to fight back and defend themselves and their families. But is “self-defence” a feasible plea in a court of law or could you be charged with murder? Carte Blanche explores your legal rights.


Script:


STRUCTURE HOME INTRUDER SHOOTINGS

VO: There are over 60 reported residential robberies across South Africa every – single –day.

LINK: No suburb is safe. It’s a highly sophisticated crime trend because of the high-risk nature of the robberies. Criminals who perpetrate home breakins - are organised. They do surveillance and come prepared – usually armed.

TSHEPO: // I will shoot you. INT1 M34

VO: TSHEPO is a former armed robber.

TSEHPO: it’s job, it’s how we eat, it’s how we get bread on the table – there is nothing we can do. INT1 M43

VO: By the age of 16, he had graduated to house robberies. More than two decades later, he’s robbed over a thousand homes.

TSHEPO: // we are doing it professionally – you will just see us standing next to you on the bed. INT1 M42

VO: But South Africans are taking up arms in self-defence, pulling the trigger on home intruders.

NEIL: I thought for family sake’s I’m not going to let these people come into my house and do anything to my family – no ways! INT1 M28

VO: Neil van Eeden lives in Umtentweni on the South Coast with his family. In February this year, he woke up to armed robbers in his home in the early morning hours.

NEIL: // they both had knives and I didn’t want to get on the other side of those knives so I was just prepared to do whatever they want just to offer them no threat and hopefully they’d leave us alone. INT1 M4

VO: Law Enforcement Expert, Lobo das Neves, says people usually go into a fight, flight or freeze mode in a robbery scenario.

LOBO: // it’s very difficult to know what your reaction will be in situation like that // if you train hard enough and you have a good understanding of the law and you know what your rights are and you know what to do – then it would be slightly than going in cold.

LINK: // with all the training and vetting required to own a gun – in the dead of the night, consumed by fear and the overwhelming need to protect your loved ones, snap decisions are made but the consequences are very real.

VO: While the robbers ransacked Neil’s house - they sent him to fetch things from the main bedroom. He then made the decision to protect his family.

NEIL: // that’s when I thought of my gun and thought sjoe, I better not because I wasn’t sure if my licence was right and then I thought know let me just do it and face the problems later

VO: He took his weapon from the safe and went back to face the robbers.

NEIL: I opened the door I walked out with the gun next to my hip – I didn’t walk out as if I was going to shoot him, I didn’t know what I was going to do, I thought maybe he would also react if he saw with the gun, he wouldn’t do anything, but he went for me rather – so just instinctively I pulled the trigger.

VO: Neil shot the robber in the stomach. After falling to ground, the wounded robber got up and fled the house - he died just up the road from the house.

Neil’s incident is not isolated. In the last 18 months there have been incidents reported in Bardene a suburb of Johannesburg, Vereeniging, Umhlanga in Durban and Lenasia.

• In January this year, an intruder was shot and wounded in Bazley on the KZN South Coast
• Four months later, an elderly woman shot & killed an intruder and wounded a second one in Pinetown, Durban.
• In May, another two intruders were shot & killed in Lynwood, Pretoria.
• And then in the same week, a father shot & killed two intruders who allegedly threatened his baby in Middleburg.

LINK: But pulling the trigger can shift the balance very quickly – within seconds you go from being the victim of a crime to a suspect in a criminal investigation – simply put, you could end up behind bars yourself.

LOBO: The moment you put pressure on the trigger – you cannot call the bullet back and you have to take full responsibility for your actions.

VO: Advocate John Welch explains there is a 90% chance that the police will arrest the homeowner.

ADV WELCH: The police arrive on the scene they find a dead or serious injured person – //, they don’t know the facts of this particular case. They are going to say I am not a judge in this matter, I am investigation this matter.

VO: Neil was not charged criminally, the case was ruled to be self-defence.

NEIL: I regret taking a young boy’s life, but the audacity to come into my house demanding this and that. // I didn’t think, my finger just pulled the trigger because he was attacking me with a knife.

VO: While Neil’s case was clear-cut, Das Neves has come across a number of cases where the crime scenes have been staged in order to claim self-defence.

LOBO: We have advance forensic science in the country - we can reconstruct that crime scene almost to a T. // even if you fired your firearm lawfully and you altered the crime scene it’s going to be very difficult to convince people that your shooting justifiable .

VO: Advocate Welch explains in terms of our current Constitution and legal framework – the limitations to self-defence claims are clear.

ADV WELCH: // that attack or unlawful invasion or attack on my property must affect life and limb as well. If it is only an invasion of property and there is no threat towards a person – then I am not entitled to // use force.

VO: But it appears that South Africans are willing to take their chances with the law, rather than the home intruders.

VOX POP 1: I would shoot him, I would definitely shoot him – I mean I am trying to protect myself.
VOX POP 2: If I have to choose between saving my family’s life and going to jail I would take the option of jail.
VOX POP 3: I wouldn’t be worried about the law, I’d be worried about my family.

LOBO: Just remember, not even the state has the right to effect capital punishment – it’s out of the constitution – we don’t kill people in this country – number two a house owner has no right to be judge, jury and executioner.

LINK: You may only shoot at an intruder if there is an imminent and unlawful threat – you can’t shoot if someone is trespassing on your property even if you assume there is danger – claiming self-defence is not a get out of jail free card.

LOBO: // there is this sense and this urban legend out there that makes people believe that once someone has gained entry into your house that you have the right to shoot them or to kill them – which is not true – your first line of action should be to arrest the person and to keep them detained until the police arrived – that’s the first course of action.

TSHEPO: the law is stupid
DEVI: if I said to you get out of my house I have a gun – what would you do? //
TSHEPO: I’m not going to listen to you because I know I am wrong inside your house. I shouldn’t be there I know. // if I see a gun I will run out or if I have mine I will shoot you first // I am going to shoot you first.
DEVI: you wont even think twice
TSEHPO: I am not going to hesitate I will shoot you first

VO: Residential robbery is a crime trend that’s spiralling out of control. Gareth Newham from the Institute for Security Studies points out there’s been almost a 40% increase since 2012.

GARETH: Because of the crisis in policing over the last decade or so – these gangs are operating with much lower levels of risk of being caught and being brought before the court.

VO: It’s a high-risk crime – even for criminals – while Tsepho has dodged many bullets, he was once shot 7 times by a homeowner. Despite the risks, it’s a lucrative line of work and his field of choice.

DEVI: Why house breaking and not hi-jacking?
TSHEPO: hijacking X5, if you hijack it they wont give you so much money – I get a R30 000 ring inside the house, I can get a watch, R50k, R100k – I go sell it they give me half price.

VO: And they don’t discriminate, anyone with wealth is a potential target says Tshepo.

TSHEPO: we go to all the areas, even to black people we go as long as we know they are driving nice cars they have nice things, we go.

VO: The average response time for security and police is 15 minutes in South Africa . A lot can happen in that time, explains Das Neves.

LOBO: Unfortunately robbers don’t follow a handbook, once they’ve entered your home – you don’t know if they just want to take your laptop, your life or both – there’s no way of predicting what they will do.

VO: But having a gun in your home is not always a guarantee that you will be able to defend yourself successfully explains Newham.

GARETH: Research shows you’re much more likely to have your firearm taken away from you in a house robbery than to effectively use it to defend yourself because they don’t let you know they are coming.

VO: And with big bounties at play – criminals like Tshepo won’t hesitate to use violence.

TSHEPO: Some of them want to show they wives ‘ek is die man’ // that’s how you die. // they must not fight back – you must surrender yourself
DEVI: Did you threaten to shoot people?
TSHEPO: yes,
DEVI: Did you shoot anybody?
TSHEPO: yes.
DEVI: Dead?
TSHEPO: I am not sure if he is dead or alive.
DEVI: how many people have you shot?
TSHEPO: I shot many times, many times, but I am not sure if they are dead or…

VO: With murder and armed robbery rates at it’s worse in the last 5 years, Newham believes the police are to blame – he says it’s not a matter of resources, but rather ineffective police leadership.

GARETH: House robberies are committed by gangs that commit robberies over and over again. You don’t have to arrest thousands of people, just a few hundred and you can reduce house robberies by a dramatic amount.

VO: But until then, it appears to be a free for all. In Neil’s case, the robber he had shot had just been released from jail having committed related crimes.

NEIL: it’s pathetic there is no rehabilitation – they go in, they come out same people even worse – they don’t rehabilitate them when they are in jail, it’s just somewhere to keep them

VO: South Africa has a high re-offense rate, Newham explains that the prison system doesn’t address the driving forces behind crime.

GARETH: In many cases prisons in SA and around the world make the problems worse, you get networked to even more serious criminals.

VO: And while crime pays, it appears that the robbers have more rights than gun-owners.

LOBO: The law weighs so heavily in the perpetrator’s favour in the house break-in situation when the house is occupied, the homeowner and the gun owner has so many things to consider.

VO: For Neil, although the ordeal has changed him, he says the decision is still a simple one.

NEIL: I am armed when I am at home, I don’t want them coming here again. // I would shoot again if my family or myself was under attack.

VO: As civilians take up arms, criminals will continued to come prepared.

TSHEPO: I have to defend myself, if I have a gun I will shoot you.














PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: While victims of home invasions are increasingly fighting back in self-defence, the legal consequences are real - you could end up behind bars facing criminal charges.

PROMO 2
VO: With residential robberies at an all time high - victims of home invasions are reacting in self-defence.

NEIL: I didn’t think, my finger just pulled the trigger because he was attacking me with a knife.

VO: We investigate the legal limitations around fighting back.

PROMO 3

VO: Everyday there are over 60 residential robberies in South Africa.

TSHEPO: // I will shoot you. It’s job, it’s how we eat, it’s how we get bread on the table .

VO: What your rights are in protecting you and your loved ones.


PROMO 4

VO: There are over 60 residential robberies in South Africa every – single – day.

It’s a lucrative but high-risk crime trend – robbers come armed.

TSHEPO: if I see a gun I will run out or if I have mine I will shoot you first // I am not going to hesitate

VO: But fighting back in self-defence could mean you go from being the victim to a suspect in a criminal investigation.

LOBO: you cannot call the bullet back and you have to take full responsibility for your actions

In the last 18 months there have been incidents reported in Bardene a suburb of Johannesburg, Vereeniging, Umhlanga in Durban and Lenasia. • In January this year, an intruder was shot and wounded in Bazley on the KZN South Coast • Four months later, an elderly woman shot & killed an intruder and wounded a second one in Pinetown, Durban. • In May, another two intruders were shot & killed in Lynwood, Pretoria. • And then in the same week, a father shot & killed two intruders who allegedly threatened his baby in Middleburg. LINK: But pulling the trigger can shift the balance very quickly – within seconds you go from being the victim of a crime to a suspect in a criminal investigation – simply put, you could end up behind bars yourself. LOBO: The moment you put pressure on the trigger – you cannot call the bullet back and you have to take full responsibility for your actions. VO: Advocate John Welch explains there is a 90% chance that the police will arrest the homeowner. ADV WELCH: The police arrive on the scene they find a dead or serious injured person – //, they don’t know the facts of this particular case. They are going to say I am not a judge in this matter, I am investigation this matter. VO: Neil was not charged criminally, the case was ruled to be self-defence. NEIL: I regret taking a young boy’s life, but the audacity to come into my house demanding this and that. // I didn’t think, my finger just pulled the trigger because he was attacking me with a knife. VO: While Neil’s case was clear-cut, Das Neves has come across a number of cases where the crime scenes have been staged in order to claim self-defence. LOBO: We have advance forensic science in the country - we can reconstruct that crime scene almost to a T. // even if you fired your firearm lawfully and you altered the crime scene it’s going to be very difficult to convince people that your shooting justifiable . VO: Advocate Welch explains in terms of our current Constitution and legal framework – the limitations to self-defence claims are clear. ADV WELCH: // that attack or unlawful invasion or attack on my property must affect life and limb as well. If it is only an invasion of property and there is no threat towards a person – then I am not entitled to // use force. VO: But it appears that South Africans are willing to take their chances with the law, rather than the home intruders. VOX POP 1: I would shoot him, I would definitely shoot him – I mean I am trying to protect myself. VOX POP 2: If I have to choose between saving my family’s life and going to jail I would take the option of jail. VOX POP 3: I wouldn’t be worried about the law, I’d be worried about my family. LOBO: Just remember, not even the state has the right to effect capital punishment – it’s out of the constitution – we don’t kill people in this country – number two a house owner has no right to be judge, jury and executioner. LINK: You may only shoot at an intruder if there is an imminent and unlawful threat – you can’t shoot if someone is trespassing on your property even if you assume there is danger – claiming self-defence is not a get out of jail free card. LOBO: // there is this sense and this urban legend out there that makes people believe that once someone has gained entry into your house that you have the right to shoot them or to kill them – which is not true – your first line of action should be to arrest the person and to keep them detained until the police arrived – that’s the first course of action. TSHEPO: the law is stupid DEVI: if I said to you get out of my house I have a gun – what would you do? // TSHEPO: I’m not going to listen to you because I know I am wrong inside your house. I shouldn’t be there I know. // if I see a gun I will run out or if I have mine I will shoot you first // I am going to shoot you first. DEVI: you wont even think twice TSEHPO: I am not going to hesitate I will shoot you first VO: Residential robbery is a crime trend that’s spiralling out of control. Gareth Newham from the Institute for Security Studies points out there’s been almost a 40% increase since 2012. GARETH: Because of the crisis in policing over the last decade or so – these gangs are operating with much lower levels of risk of being caught and being brought before the court. VO: It’s a high-risk crime – even for criminals – while Tsepho has dodged many bullets, he was once shot 7 times by a homeowner. Despite the risks, it’s a lucrative line of work and his field of choice. DEVI: Why house breaking and not hi-jacking? TSHEPO: hijacking X5, if you hijack it they wont give you so much money – I get a R30 000 ring inside the house, I can get a watch, R50k, R100k – I go sell it they give me half price. VO: And they don’t discriminate, anyone with wealth is a potential target says Tshepo. TSHEPO: we go to all the areas, even to black people we go as long as we know they are driving nice cars they have nice things, we go. VO: The average response time for security and police is 15 minutes in South Africa . A lot can happen in that time, explains Das Neves. LOBO: Unfortunately robbers don’t follow a handbook, once they’ve entered your home – you don’t know if they just want to take your laptop, your life or both – there’s no way of predicting what they will do. VO: But having a gun in your home is not always a guarantee that you will be able to defend yourself successfully explains Newham. GARETH: Research shows you’re much more likely to have your firearm taken away from you in a house robbery than to effectively use it to defend yourself because they don’t let you know they are coming. VO: And with big bounties at play – criminals like Tshepo won’t hesitate to use violence. TSHEPO: Some of them want to show they wives ‘ek is die man’ // that’s how you die. // they must not fight back – you must surrender yourself DEVI: Did you threaten to shoot people? TSHEPO: yes, DEVI: Did you shoot anybody? TSHEPO: yes. DEVI: Dead? TSHEPO: I am not sure if he is dead or alive. DEVI: how many people have you shot? TSHEPO: I shot many times, many times, but I am not sure if they are dead or… VO: With murder and armed robbery rates at it’s worse in the last 5 years, Newham believes the police are to blame – he says it’s not a matter of resources, but rather ineffective police leadership. GARETH: House robberies are committed by gangs that commit robberies over and over again. You don’t have to arrest thousands of people, just a few hundred and you can reduce house robberies by a dramatic amount. VO: But until then, it appears to be a free for all. In Neil’s case, the robber he had shot had just been released from jail having committed related crimes. NEIL: it’s pathetic there is no rehabilitation – they go in, they come out same people even worse – they don’t rehabilitate them when they are in jail, it’s just somewhere to keep them VO: South Africa has a high re-offense rate, Newham explains that the prison system doesn’t address the driving forces behind crime. GARETH: In many cases prisons in SA and around the world make the problems worse, you get networked to even more serious criminals. VO: And while crime pays, it appears that the robbers have more rights than gun-owners. LOBO: The law weighs so heavily in the perpetrator’s favour in the house break-in situation when the house is occupied, the homeowner and the gun owner has so many things to consider. VO: For Neil, although the ordeal has changed him, he says the decision is still a simple one. NEIL: I am armed when I am at home, I don’t want them coming here again. // I would shoot again if my family or myself was under attack. VO: As civilians take up arms, criminals will continued to come prepared. TSHEPO: I have to defend myself, if I have a gun I will shoot you. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: While victims of home invasions are increasingly fighting back in self-defence, the legal consequences are real - you could end up behind bars facing criminal charges. PROMO 2 VO: With residential robberies at an all time high - victims of home invasions are reacting in self-defence. NEIL: I didn’t think, my finger just pulled the trigger because he was attacking me with a knife. VO: We investigate the legal limitations around fighting back. PROMO 3 VO: Everyday there are over 60 residential robberies in South Africa. TSHEPO: // I will shoot you. It’s job, it’s how we eat, it’s how we get bread on the table . VO: What your rights are in protecting you and your loved ones. PROMO 4 VO: There are over 60 residential robberies in South Africa every – single – day. It’s a lucrative but high-risk crime trend – robbers come armed. TSHEPO: if I see a gun I will run out or if I have mine I will shoot you first // I am not going to hesitate VO: But fighting back in self-defence could mean you go from being the victim to a suspect in a criminal investigation. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A Home Intruder Shooting is not always straight-forward self-defenses scenario – pulling the trigger could land you behind bars.
metadata.Summary: With armed home robberies up by 7.3% in last year’s National Crime Statistics, South Africans are stepping up to defend their families and their homes. But self-defense is not a get out of jail free claim – you could actually end up behind bars if you act outside of the law. We ask where is the line and when do you cross it according to the law.
metadata.Further information: With a spate of home intruder shootings, we explore the legal debate around what is considered self-defense and what is murder in the eyes of the law. We explore the current state of house robberies in South Africa, looking at this rising crime trend and driving forces behind it. A number of the intruders that have been killed have been identified as criminals that have been released from prison just weeks before committing the crimes that lead to their death. We look at what appears to be a vicious crime circle, where criminals get caught, justice is thought to be served, yet the criminals continue to perpetrate more crimes. EXPERT INTERVIEWS - Gareth Newham – ISS – will paint the picture of current crime trend, driving forces and why South Africans are so desperately vulnerable in the context of violent crime. - Lobo das Neves – Law Enforcement Expert – will explain how people react, how they should react – and expand on the flight or fright theories. - Advocate John Welch – legal expert – will explain the legal framework, what action can be taken and what the consequences are for homeowners who shoot outside of the law. CASE STUDIES There are at least 5 cases since January this year of intruders being shot by residents of the homes that were being burgled. In some cases the home owners have been charged, in some cases where there were clear cases of self-defense no charges were laid. Some of the more recent case studies are either too traumatized to speak or are concerned about the pending criminal investigations. CASE STUDY PORT SHEPSTONE February 8, 2018 Two men armed with knives and a screw-driver broke into a home in Park Road, Umtentweni during the early hours. Neil and Lynn-Dee van Eeden and their 17-year-old son, Josh were sleeping when the men quietly cut the burglar bars with bolt-cutters and climbed through the lounge window into the house and proceeded to make their way down the passage and into Neil’s bedroom. Neil woke-up with the two men, wearing hats, in his bedroom, telling him to ‘keep cool’. One of the men had one of Neil’s socks wrapped around his face. When the family’s boerboel come through to the bedroom, the intruders attempted to stab the dog. A calm Neil asked the men if he could put the dog in his bedroom. They agreed, and made their way to Joshua’s room where they helped themselves to his laptop and cellphone. They demanded money, and asked Neil for a bag. When the men realised they had taken only one of a pair of takkies, they insisted that Neil retrieve the other from the bedroom. Deciding enough was enough, Neil went back into his bedroom, closed the door to keep the dogs inside, and took his gun from the safe. When the intruder saw the gun, he went for me and that’s when I shot him. This is what worried me – if they couldn’t find money what would they have done, tied us up and slit our throats? – Neil. Neil said the injured man stumbled back and fell into Josh’s room, where he lay for a while. The wounded man staggered into Josh’s room, were he lay for a while. The other man, who was busy filling the bag with laptops, clothes and other household goods, abandoned the bag, opened the sliding door in the lounge and fled. By this time, Lynn-Dee had emerged from her bedroom to see the wounded man stumbling down the passage, shouting ‘please don’t shoot me, please don’t shoot me…’ “Out of sheer fright, Josh and I grabbed coffee cups and threw them at him,” said Lynn-Dee. Lynn-Dee phoned her level-headed friend Sally Heaver for help, just before 3am. The missing takkie which provided the chance for Neil to retrieve his firearm. Sally in turn quickly contacted the police and posted a message on a local WhatsApp group saying the family needed help. Police spokesman, Vincent Pandarum said the wounded man had managed to run a few hundred metres before collapsing and dying. Reflecting on the ordeal, Lynn-Dee said the men were starting to get aggressive as things weren’t going as planned – suddenly there were dogs, no money, not everyone in the same room and it was taking longer than anticipated. One of the coffee cups thrown at the intruder. Josh hadn’t seen his mother during this ordeal and was worried that she had been targeted. “It could have been so much worse,” added Josh. Capt Pandarum said a case of house robbery would be investigated, and an inquest docket opened in relation to the death of the suspect. No arrests have been made at this stage.
